cards.front: Why does UV light start radical substitution of an alkane with chlorine?
cards.back: UV light supplies energy to break the Cl–Cl bond **homolytically**, giving two chlorine radicals. These radicals can then attack alkane molecules.
cards.hint: Ask what splits first, before any alkane reacts.

cards.front: What are the three stages of radical substitution, in order?
cards.back: **Initiation** splits Cl2 into radicals using UV light. **Propagation** steps use radicals and make a new radical each time. **Termination** combines two radicals, so no radical is made.
cards.hint: Think about start, repeat, and stop.

cards.back: A **radical** is a species with an unpaired electron. It is shown with a dot on the atom that has that electron.
cards.hint: Look for the dot in the formula.

cards.back: **Homolytic fission** breaks a covalent bond so that each bonded atom takes one of the bonding electrons, forming two radicals.
cards.hint: Each atom gets one electron, not both.

cards.front: Write the initiation step for chlorination of methane, and say what the label above the arrow means.
cards.back: $\mathrm{Cl_2 \xrightarrow{UV} 2Cl\cdot}$. The **UV** above the arrow is the energy source, not a reactant.
cards.hint: Cl2 is the only molecule that splits here.

cards.front: What two propagation steps regenerate a chlorine radical in methane chlorination?
cards.back: First $\mathrm{Cl\cdot + CH_4 \rightarrow HCl + CH_3\cdot}$, then $\mathrm{CH_3\cdot + Cl_2 \rightarrow CH_3Cl + Cl\cdot}$. The second step gives back a chlorine radical.
cards.hint: Track which radical is used up and which is made.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say UV light splits methane to start this reaction?
cards.back: UV light splits **chlorine** molecules first, not methane. The chlorine radicals then remove hydrogen from methane.
cards.hint: Which molecule absorbs the UV energy?

cards.front: What happens in a termination step?
cards.back: Two radicals combine to form a **covalent bond**, and no new radical is produced. For example, Cl· + Cl· gives Cl2.
cards.hint: Count the radicals before and after.

cards.front: Can methane chlorination be assumed to give only chloromethane?
cards.back: No. Further substitution of chloromethane can occur, so the product can be a **mixture**. Two methyl radicals can also combine to form ethane.
cards.hint: Think about what the product can react with next.

cards.back: A **fish-hook** arrow is a single-headed curved arrow that shows the movement of one electron.
cards.hint: Count the heads on the arrow.

cards.front: How does a fish-hook arrow differ from a full-headed curly arrow?
cards.back: A **fish-hook** arrow is single-headed and shows one electron. A full-headed arrow shows a movement of an electron pair.

cards.front: How many fish-hook arrows show homolytic fission of Cl2, and where do they point?
cards.back: **Two** arrows start from the Cl–Cl bond, one pointing to each chlorine atom. Each atom receives one electron, giving 2Cl·.
